opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it taught me that my limits were both further out and closer in than I'd assumed, depending on which dimension you look at.

On the raw-hours side, you can push surprisingly far when you care deeply about what you're doing. There was a stretch where I was doing research during the day, working on Climate Science in the evenings and on weekends, and trying to keep up with coursework somewhere in between. You find that you can run like that for a while, and it feels almost energizing at first, because everything is moving.

But the thing I learned is that the bottleneck isn't really time, it's attention. You can split your hours three ways, but you can't really split your deep focus three ways and expect to do world-class work in any of them. Research, especially the kind of research I cared about, requires you to hold a problem in your head for days or weeks. Starting something, even a nonprofit, requires the same thing. When you're context-switching constantly, you end up doing a decent job at many things instead of an exceptional job at one.

So eventually I had to be honest with myself and make choices. University was the obvious thing to drop, because I felt I was learning far more by doing actual research than by sitting in lectures. And over time I realized that the thing I most wanted to go all-in on was building toward more capable AI systems, because I believed that if you get that right, it becomes leverage for everything else, including problems like climate.

The other lesson was about sustainability. You can sprint, but you need to know you're sprinting. If you treat a sprint like it's your normal pace, you burn out, and you also stop thinking clearly about what actually matters. So I came out of that period with a much stronger instinct for focus: pick the one thing, go extremely deep, and say no to a lot of genuinely good opportunities.

r001.rationale: The response says he struggled to give deep focus to three commitments and eventually chose to drop university, but it never states that he concluded his capacity was limited to two simultaneous major commitments.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it taught me that I don't have as many limits as I thought, but the ones I do have are real, and they don't care how motivated you are.

At the time, I was doing my degree in Vienna, I was a research scientist at FAIR working on Pluribus-adjacent stuff, poker AI, and I was running Climate Science, which was a nonprofit with a few hundred volunteers across the world. And for a while I genuinely believed I could just do all three at full intensity. I'd wake up at five, do research until classes, go to lectures, come back, do calls with the climate team across time zones until midnight. And it worked. For about a year it actually worked, and that was the dangerous part, because it convinced me the model was fine.

What broke wasn't my output, it was the quality of my thinking. Research needs these long, uninterrupted stretches where you sit with a problem and let it be confusing. I was never confused for long enough. I was context-switching every two hours, and I noticed I'd started doing the thing where you execute the obvious next step on each project rather than asking whether it's the right step. That's a very subtle failure mode. Nobody around you sees it. You look productive. You feel productive. But you've quietly become a worse researcher and a worse founder at the same time.

So the real lesson was that my limit isn't hours. It's the number of things I can care about at the depth that actually matters. I think that number for me is one, maybe one and a half. And I'd rather be the person who's all in on one thing than the person who's impressive on paper across three. That's a big part of why, when we started Magic, I was extremely unwilling to run anything on the side. I'd learned the hard way that "on the side" is a lie you tell yourself.

The other thing, and this is less flattering, is that I learned I'm not good at stopping. Someone else had to basically tell me, you're going to hurt yourself and the people depending on you. I didn't notice from the inside. So now I try to build in people who are allowed to say that to me, because I know I won't see it coming.

r001.rationale: The response says his capacity for deeply caring about things was “one, maybe one and a half,” not two simultaneous major commitments.

astra-6.text:
It taught me that being excited about everything doesn’t mean you can do everything at once. I was trying to balance university, research at FAIR, and starting Climate Science, and I underestimated how much attention each of those needed. You can work more hours for a while, but you can’t keep adding commitments and expect the quality of everything to stay the same.

The hard part was accepting that prioritizing means giving up something you actually want to do. It’s easy to say no to things you don’t care about. It’s much harder when every opportunity feels worthwhile. I had to get more honest with myself about my capacity and decide where I could really contribute.

r001.rationale: The response says he could not handle every commitment at once and needed to prioritize, but it does not state that his capacity was limited to two simultaneous major commitments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it taught me that being interested in several things doesn’t mean you can give all of them the attention they deserve at the same time. University, research at FAIR, and starting Climate Science could each take as much time as I was willing to put into them. Working longer hours wasn’t going to resolve that.

The difficult part was accepting the trade-offs. You can care about something and still decide that you’re not the right person to do it, or that now isn’t the right time. For me, the lesson was to be more deliberate about where I could contribute most, and to be honest about what I could actually commit to.

r001.rationale: The response says he could not give several commitments the attention they deserved at once, but it never states that his capacity was limited to two simultaneous major commitments.
